analysis.one_liner: Ends the tax break that lets the ultra-wealthy shelter investment gains inside custom life insurance policies.
analysis.headline: The bill has gone nowhere: introduced in April 2026 with no cosponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has received no action.
analysis.plain_summary: Very wealthy people can buy custom, privately placed life insurance and annuity contracts that wrap their investment portfolios. Because the wrapper counts as life insurance, the investment income inside it compounds tax-free — a break ordinary retirement savers with ordinary insurance policies cannot get at this scale. This bill says those private placement contracts no longer count as insurance for tax purposes, so the investment income is taxed as it is earned, and it adds strict reporting rules with heavy penalties for insurers who fail to file.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: the tax base is protected because wealthy investors can no longer shelter investment gains inside insurance wrappers, and the broader tax code treats similar income the same way for everyone. The bill also raises revenue indirectly by bringing that income onto the tax rolls. Ordinary savers gain nothing directly, but they stop effectively subsidizing a shelter only the very rich can access.

how_it_helps.text: It ends the treatment of certain privately placed life insurance and annuity contracts as insurance for tax purposes, so the wealthy investors who buy them are taxed on the income from the underlying investments as it accrues, just like other investors.
It covers foreign-issued contracts held by US persons, closing the route of parking investments in offshore life-insurance wrappers to escape US tax.
It requires annual reporting on these contracts and creates new information-sharing rules under FATCA for offshore insurers, with penalties starting at $1 million for failures to report.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy households currently using private placement life insurance, who would owe tax on investment income as it accrues, and the insurers and reinsurers that sell these contracts, who face new reporting duties and million-dollar penalties for noncompliance.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden is heavy: issuers and reinsurers must file detailed initial and annual returns on every contract, and face a $1 million penalty plus another $1 million for each 30 days a missed initial report goes uncorrected, plus disclosure obligations to regulators and in SEC filings.

The rules apply to contracts already in existence, not just new ones, so investors who relied on the old tax treatment of existing policies must unwind or convert them within 180 days of enactment to avoid the new rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — closing a shelter used by the richest households — is real and the revenue belongs in the tax base everyone else supports. The cost is a heavier compliance load on insurance issuers and reinsurers, including new reporting and large penalties. The bill is technically complex and applies retroactively to existing contracts (with a 180-day exit window), which insurers would argue is disruptive; but the core design is targeted at a genuine tax gap, not overbroad.

outcome.mechanism: Wyden introduced it and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no further action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 13, 2026, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance.
Since the referral, the action history shows no markup, no vote, and no further movement.
No senators have signed on as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won yet; for now, the wealthy investors and insurers who benefit from the PPLI tax treatment are untouched, and the tax revenue the bill would raise remains uncollected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; the shelter remains untouched

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-OR), Ranking Member of Senate Finance
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip favorable tax treatment from private placement life insurance contracts and to require reporting on them.

sides.party_line_note: No one has taken a recorded position except the sponsor; no cosponsors and no votes yet.

industries.industry: Private placement life insurance issuers and offshore insurers/reinsurers
industries.note: The bill strips the tax advantage that makes PPLI products attractive to ultra-wealthy clients, treating the contracts as ordinary investment accounts for tax purposes and imposing new reporting duties with $1 million-scale penalties. Their wealthy customers would have much less reason to buy.

These investors would lose the ability to compound investment income inside a life insurance wrapper free of tax. Ordinary taxpayers cannot use these products, which are sold only to people meeting high income, asset, or credential thresholds.

Traditional retail life insurance keeps its tax treatment; only the private placement segment is targeted. Some large insurers with offshore or reinsurance arms would face new compliance and reporting obligations.

analysis.trajectory: As a tax bill that raises revenue from insurers and ultra-wealthy investors with no cosponsors, it faces the usual path of such proposals: it would need the Finance Committee to take it up and would more realistically move only if attached to a broader tax package championed by leadership. With the Senate narrowly divided and no Republican or other Democratic support on record, odds of standalone passage this Congress are low.
